Testimony of Rep. Adam Lee presenting
LD 273, An Act toPreserve Legislative Authority over Investigating
Committees
Before the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government, I am Adam Lee, and I represent House District 89
which is Downtown Auburn and New Auburn. Pm here to introduce LD 273, An Act to Preserve
Legislative Authority over Investigating Committees.
We are the Legislature. We are a co-equal branch of govermnent. We are the primary policy-
making body in Maine's Government. The first Article in the Maine Constitution, Article IV, devoted to a branch of govermnent, is not devoted to the executive nor the judiciary; it is devoted
to us, the Legislature. We are the representative branch of government. We are the closest to the
people. As the U.S. Supreme Court in United States v. Rumely noted in 1953, that is why
legislative bodies are imbued with the power to subpoena, because as the Court said, "[i]t is the proper duty of a representative body to look diligently into every affair of government and talk
much about what it sees. It ismeant to the be the eyes and voice and to embody the wisdom and will of its constituents." That's why we -- the Legislature -- are the sole body with the authority to
provide a committee subpoena power.
Why are we so willing to give it away without ensuring that we maintain some control over the entities to whom we provide the power? Why are we willing to give up the power
without ensuring that we remain the eyes and voice of the govermnent? When we do so and provide our authority to others, we abandon our role in government, we abandon our constituents, and we cease to embody their wisdom and will.
This bill is not partisan. This bill is not a criticism of any prior committee nor of the chief
executive. This bill is highly critical, however, of Legislatures. Whether that's we who sit here in Augusta or Congress in DC, this is a national and state problem. When the representative
legislative branch of govermnent rolls over and ceases to exercise its power, the void will be filled by an Executive. This bill calls for one thing: that we, the Legislature, understand the
collective power we have as a body -- and ensure that we exercise it. Very simply, this bill

ensures that when the legislature provides a committee subpoena power, the Legislature shall then have the power to determine the membership and scope of that committee.
We're talking first principles here. As James Madison said in Federalist 51, "in republican govermnent, the legislative authority necessarily predominates." He further explained how we should exercise that authority. "[T]he great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers in the same department, consists in giving to those who administer each
department the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachment of
the others." He went on, "[t]he provision for defense. . .must. . .be made commensurate to the danger of the attack. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
It is perfectly natural for the executive branch to seek the subpoena power for committees it creates. It's also perfectly natural for this body to check that ambition by exercising our power
and authority and insisting, in such circumstances, that we embody the wisdom and will of our
constituents and remain their eyes and voice, diligently looking into every affair of government. I'd be happy to answer your questions and be available for the Work session to assist in working
this bill.

Testimony in Support of LD 273: "An Act to Preserve Legislative Authority over Investigating Committees"
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and the distinguished members of the Committee on State and Local Government, my name is Harris Van Pate and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. LD 273 is a necessary measure to reinforce the constitutional separation of powers in Maine and to ensure that the legislative branch's authority remains intact in conducting investigations and oversight.
The Maine Legislature, as the duly elected representative body of the people, must retain complete control over its investigative committees without undue interference from other branches of government. This bill clarifies and codifies that authority, strengthening the ability of lawmakers to conduct transparent and accountable inquiries into matters of public interest.
Upholding the Principles of Representative Government
At its core, LD 273 ensures that the legislative branch maintains its essential function as a check on the executive branch and state agencies. The Maine Constitution vests legislative power in the Senate and House of Representatives, which includes the ability to conduct inquiries, issue subpoenas, and gather testimony in pursuit of the public interest. Any efforts to erode this authority undermine the foundational principles of representative government and transparency. Even in the federal legislature, the power to oversee investigations is certain.1
Historical precedent and constitutional interpretation affirm that state legislatures must be able to investigate issues affecting their constituents, whether those relate to government inefficiencies, misuse of public funds, or policy failures, and these powers of legislative oversight are widespread throughout the United States.2 LD 273 provides a necessary safeguard to ensure that legislative committees can operate effectively and without obstruction.
Preventing Overreach and Preserving Legislative Independence

In recent years, there has been a troubling trend of executive overreach and bureaucratic stonewalling in response to legislative investigations.3 4 Ensuring the Legislature has clear statutory backing for its investigative committees is essential to preventing such encroachments on legislative independence. If legislative authority is diminished, so is the public's ability to hold their government accountable.
LD 273 does not create new powers for the Legislature but rather affirms its existing constitutional role. This is especially important in cases where state agencies or officials may be reluctant to cooperate with oversight efforts. Without a strong and independent investigatory function, the ability of lawmakers to fulfill their duty to Maine citizens is significantly weakened.
Aligning Maine with Best Practices in Government Oversight
Many states have similar laws that explicitly affirm legislative authority over investigating committees, recognizing the importance of robust oversight in maintaining good governance.5 Maine should follow suit by passing LD 273 to ensure that our legislative committees have the necessary tools to conduct their work unimpeded.
This bill aligns with the responsible and limited government principles for which Maine Policy Institute has long advocated. Accountability and transparency are hallmarks of a government that serves the people rather than politicians. A strong legislative investigatory function is crucial to ensuring that taxpayer dollars are spent efficiently, and that state government remains responsive to the people of Maine.
Conclusion
For these reasons, the Maine Policy Institute strongly supports LD 273. We urge this committee to vote "Ought to Pass" and reaffirm the Legislature's role as the primary investigatory body within state government. This is a critical step toward ensuring transparency, accountability, and the preservation of constitutional principles in Maine.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
